group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
An 83-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department late in the afternoon by a neighbor who noticed that the patient, normally able to walk her small terrier three blocks without assistance, became markedly winded after only half a block and had spent the past night propped upright in a recliner because lying flat worsened her cough and shortness of breath; the neighbor also reported hearing intermittent groans when the patient tried to clear thick sputum that had become blood-tinged earlier in the day. The patient lives alone in a one-story bungalow, pays her own bills, and usually prepares her own meals, though she keeps pillboxes filled by her daughter for a chronic dilated ventricular condition that was discovered eight years earlier following an episode of pedal edema and exertional dyspnea—her last cardiology visit six months ago documented an ejection fraction of 30 % and she has since remained on carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily, and a morning dose of furosemide 20 mg; she has never required device therapy or intravenous inotropes. She has no history of kidney stones, nephrotic syndrome, or dialysis, and her most recent outpatient chemistry panel three weeks ago showed a creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL and blood urea nitrogen in the mid-teens. She denies hepatitis, jaundice, heavy alcohol use, or prior abdominal imaging suggestive of chronic liver disease, and she has never undergone oncologic surgery, radiation, or chemotherapy. Influenza vaccination was obtained at a local pharmacy five weeks earlier; pneumococcal immunization was completed two years ago. She quit smoking thirty years ago after a 10-pack-year exposure, drinks half a glass of wine with dinner on Sundays, and has never used illicit drugs. The illness started four days prior with chills, diffuse myalgias, and a dry cough; by the second day the cough became productive of yellow sputum and she noted temperatures on her digital tympanic thermometer as high as 38.8 °C, managed only with a single 500 mg dose of acetaminophen. On the morning of presentation she experienced a shaking chill and felt “dizzy” when she tried to stand, prompting the neighbor’s call to emergency services. In the prehospital phase no oxygen or fluids were administered so that baseline measurements could be captured. Upon arrival in triage she was sitting forward, using accessory neck muscles to breathe but able to answer questions appropriately; initial vitals prior to any treatment revealed an oral temperature of 39.5 °C, regular tachycardia at 107 beats per minute, a narrow pulse pressure with cuff readings of 97/58 mm Hg confirmed manually, tachypnea at 38 breaths per minute with shallow excursions, and fingertip pulse oximetry of 84 % while breathing ambient air. Her skin was warm, flushed, and dry; jugular venous pulsation rose to the level of the clavicle when the head of the bed was at 45°, similar to prior heart-failure clinic notes, and trace bilateral ankle edema was present but unchanged from baseline according to the daughter’s description. Cardiac examination disclosed a rapid S1 and S2 with a low-frequency third sound best heard at the apex and no appreciable murmurs or pericardial rub. Pulmonary auscultation demonstrated coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower third of the posterior thorax with near absence of breath sounds below the scapular tip and dullness to percussion along the same region, whereas the left fields transmitted vesicular sounds with only scattered late crackles at the base. Abdominal palpation was soft and nontender with normal bowel sounds and no hepatosplenomegaly. There was no calf tenderness or asymmetric swelling. Point-of-care capillary glucose obtained before intravenous access measured 145 mg/dL. An arterial blood sample while she continued on room air showed pH 7.51, PaCO₂ 28 mm Hg, PaO₂ 59 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, consistent with an acute respiratory alkalosis driven by hyperventilation and significant hypoxemia. Venous chemistry drawn simultaneously revealed sodium 151 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, chloride 108 mEq/L, bicarbonate concordant with the blood gas, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and serum glucose reconfirmed at 145 mg/dL. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 17.2 × 10⁹/L with 86 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 28 %, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, and platelets 190 × 10⁹/L. High-sensitivity troponin-T was below the assay threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph performed before any fluids, antibiotics, or diuretics depicted a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a layered meniscus measuring approximately 2 cm in depth along the right costophrenic angle, while cardiac silhouette and mediastinum matched prior outpatient films. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia at 106 beats per minute with left bundle branch block identical to baseline and no new ischemic changes. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and urine antigens for Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae were obtained prior to therapy. Up to this point no antipyretics beyond the remote home dose, no vasoactive agents, no intravenous fluids, and no supplemental oxygen had been given, preserving her presenting hemodynamics and laboratory profile for risk stratification.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI/PORT), using pretreatment findings:
- Demographics: for a woman, age minus 10 = 83 − 10 = 73. She lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: heart failure with EF 30% adds 10. No neoplastic, liver, cerebrovascular, or renal disease is documented (0 each).
- Examination: respiratory rate 38/min (≥30) adds 20. Mentation is normal (0); systolic BP 97 is not <90 mmHg (0); temperature 39.5°C is neither <35 nor ≥40°C (0); pulse 107 is not ≥125/min (0).
- Laboratory findings: BUN 38 mg/dL (≥30) adds 20; hematocrit 28% (<30%) adds 10; room-air PaO₂ 59 mmHg (<60) adds 10. SpO₂ 84% reflects the same hypoxemia and is not scored twice. Arterial pH 7.51 is not <7.35 (0); sodium 151 is not <130 mEq/L (0); glucose 145 is not ≥250 mg/dL (0).
- Imaging: the right costophrenic meniscus indicates a pleural effusion → 10.
Total = 73 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 153 (risk class V).
Final answer: 153
